concepts: Lagrange's mean value theorem and bounds on a function
questions.question: Let the function $f:[-7,0]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[-7,0]$ and differentiable on $(-7,0)$. If $f(-7)=-3$ and $f'(x)\le 2$ for all $x\in(-7,0)$, then for all such functions $f$, $f(-1)+f(0)$ lies in the interval:
questions.key_idea: LMVT on $[-7,0]$ and on $[-7,-1]$ bounds each value above; there is no lower bound.
solution: Nothing bounds $f$ from below (only $f'\le2$ is given), so the sum can be arbitrarily negative.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take $g(x)=f(x)-2x$: then $g'\le0$, so $g$ is non-increasing and bounded above by $g(-7)$.
solution: Let $g(x)=f(x)-2x$. Then $g'(x)=f'(x)-2\le0$ on $(-7,0)$, so $g$ is non-increasing on $[-7,0]$.
Hence $f(-1)+f(0)\le 20$; the bound is attained by $f(x)=2x+11$ (check: $f(-7)=-3$).
For the other side take $f(x)=-3-N(x+7)$ with $N$ large: $f(-1)+f(0)=-6-13N\to-\infty$, so the range is $(-\infty,20]$.

useful_results: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable inside and $f'\le M$, then $f(x)-f(a)\le M(x-a)$ for every $x\in[a,b]$ (one-sided Lipschitz bound from LMVT).
Upper bounds of this kind add: bound each value separately from the same base point, then sum.
With only an upper bound on $f'$ the sum has no lower bound, so the answer is a half-line $(-\infty,U]$, never a closed interval.
Here $f(x)=2x+11$ attains $20$, so the bound is sharp ($f(-1)+f(0)=9+11$).

concepts: Concavity and slopes of chords of a graph
questions.question: Let $f$ be any function continuous on $[a,b]$ and twice differentiable on $(a,b)$. If for all $x\in(a,b)$, $f'(x)>0$ and $f''(x)<0$, then for $c\in(a,b)$, $\frac{f(c)-f(a)}{f(b)-f(c)}$ is greater than:
questions.key_idea: $f'>0,\ f''<0$ means an increasing concave graph, so chord slopes fall from left to right.
solution: $f'(x)>0$ and $f''(x)<0$ on $(a,b)$: the graph is increasing and concave (bends downward).
For a concave graph the chord to the left of $C$ is steeper: $m_{AC}>m_{CB}$.
As $f$ is increasing, $f(b)-f(c)>0$ and $b-c>0$; cross-multiplying gives $\frac{f(c)-f(a)}{f(b)-f(c)}>\frac{c-a}{b-c}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test-function elimination: a linear $f$ gives equality for (A), and a concrete concave $f$ such as $\sqrt{x}$ shows only (A) is always smaller.
solution: The answer must hold for every admissible $f$, so test one: $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ ($f'>0$, $f''<0$) with $a=1,\ c=3,\ b=9$.
(C) $\frac{b+a}{b-a}=\frac{10}{8}=1.25$ and (D) $1$ are both larger than $0.577$: rejected.
Only (A) survives, and the chord-slope argument shows (A) is true in general. Same answer.

useful_results: For $a<c<b$: if $f$ is concave, $\frac{f(c)-f(a)}{c-a}\ge\frac{f(b)-f(c)}{b-c}$ (strict for strictly concave); the inequality reverses for convex $f$.
Equivalent form (LMVT): $f'(\xi_1)>f'(\xi_2)$ for some $\xi_1<c<\xi_2$, since $f'$ is decreasing when $f''<0$.
Linear $f$ gives equality, so any inequality of this type is the strict version of the linear case.
Check: $f=\ln x$, $a=1,c=3,b=9$: $\frac{\ln3}{\ln3}=1>\frac13$.

concepts: Monotonicity and maximum value of a function on an interval
questions.question: If $m$ is the minimum value of $k$ for which the function $f(x)=x\sqrt{kx-x^2}$ is increasing in the interval $[0,3]$ and $M$ is the maximum value of $f$ in $[0,3]$ when $k=m$, then the ordered pair $(m,M)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $f'\ge0$ reduces to $3k\ge4x$ on $[0,3]$, so $k\ge4$; an increasing $f$ peaks at the right end.
solution: The denominator is positive, so we need $3kx^2-4x^3\ge0$, i.e. $3k-4x\ge0$ for $x\in(0,3]$.
So $3k\ge4x$ for all $x\in[0,3]$; the worst case is $x=3$: $3k\ge12$.
$f'\ge0$ on $[0,3]$, so $f$ is increasing and its maximum is at $x=3$: $M=3\sqrt{12-9}=3\sqrt3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For $f\ge0$, $f$ and $f^2$ increase together, so work with the polynomial $h=f^2=kx^3-x^4$ and avoid the square root.
solution: Since $f\ge0$, $f$ is increasing exactly when $h(x)=f(x)^2=kx^3-x^4$ is increasing.
For $k=4$, $h(x)=4x^3-x^4$ is increasing on $[0,3]$ (its derivative $x^2(12-4x)\ge0$) with $h(3)=108-81=27$.

useful_results: For a non-negative function, $f$ and $f^2$ have the same monotonicity, so a radical can be dropped before differentiating.
If $f$ is increasing on $[a,b]$, its maximum is $f(b)$ and its minimum $f(a)$; no need to solve $f'=0$ inside.
'Minimum $k$ for which $f'\ge0$ on an interval' reduces to a bound for $k$ at the worst point of the interval: here $k\ge\max\frac{4x}{3}=4$.
Check the domain too: $kx-x^2\ge0$ on $[0,3]$ needs only $k\ge3$, weaker than $k\ge4$.

questions.question: If $y(a)=\sqrt{2\left(\frac{\tan a+\cot a}{1+\tan^2 a}\right)+\frac{1}{\sin^2 a}}$, $a\in\left(\frac{3\pi}{4},\pi\right)$, then $\frac{dy}{da}$ at $a=\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is:
questions.key_idea: The radicand is a perfect square: $y=|1+\cot a|$, and on $(3\pi/4,\pi)$ the sign inside is negative.
solution: $\tan a+\cot a=\frac{\sin a}{\cos a}+\frac{\cos a}{\sin a}$ and $1+\tan^2a=\sec^2a$.
So $\frac{\tan a+\cot a}{\sec^2a}=\cos^2a\cdot\frac{1}{\sin a\cos a}=\cot a$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate $y^2$ implicitly before simplifying, then use the sign of $1+\cot a$ at the given point.

useful_results: $\sqrt{u^2}=|u|$: always fix the sign of $u$ on the stated interval before differentiating.
$\tan a+\cot a=\frac{1}{\sin a\cos a}=\frac{2}{\sin2a}$ and $\frac{\tan a+\cot a}{1+\tan^2a}=\cot a$.
$2\cot a+\csc^2a=(1+\cot a)^2$ because $\csc^2a=1+\cot^2a$.

On $\left(\frac{3\pi}{4},\pi\right)$, $\cot a<-1$, which is why the modulus opens with a minus sign. Numerical check: $y(5\pi/6)=\sqrt3-1\approx0.732$ and $2\cot a+\csc^2a\approx-3.464+4=0.536=0.732^2$.

concepts: Critical points of a polynomial function
questions.question: Suppose $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree four, having critical points at $-1,\ 0,\ 1$. If $T=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\mid f(x)=f(0)\}$, then the sum of squares of all the elements of $T$ is:
questions.key_idea: A quartic's $f'$ is a cubic, so its three critical points fix $f'(x)=Ax(x^2-1)$ up to a constant.
solution: $f$ has degree 4, so $f'$ is a cubic with roots $-1,0,1$: $f'(x)=A(x+1)(x-1)x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $f'$ is odd, so $f$ is even; then $f(x)-f(0)=x^2(px^2+q)$ and the critical point at $1$ fixes $q=-2p$.
solution: $f'$ has roots $-1,0,1$ and degree 3, so $f'$ is odd; hence $f(x)=px^4+qx^2+r$ is even.
Roots: $x=0$ (double, counted once in the set $T$) and $x^2=2$.
$T=\{0,\pm\sqrt2\}$ and the sum of squares is $0+2+2=4$. Same answer.

useful_results: A polynomial whose derivative is odd is even (plus a constant), and conversely; critical points symmetric about $0$ signal an even quartic.
If $f'(x)=A\prod(x-r_i)$, then $f(x)-f(r_0)=\int_{r_0}^{x}f'$ factors with a double root at every critical point $r_0$ where it is the base point.
$T$ is a set: a repeated root (here $x=0$, double) is counted once in the sum of squares.

concepts: Local maxima and minima of a function (first derivative test)
questions.question: If $x=1$ is a critical point of the function $f(x)=(3x^2+ax-2-a)e^x$, then:
options: $x=1$ is a local minima and $x=-\frac23$ is a local maxima of $f$.
$x=1$ is a local maxima and $x=-\frac23$ is a local minima of $f$.
$x=1$ and $x=-\frac23$ is a local maxima of $f$.
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)=e^x\cdot q(x)$, so $f'(1)=0$ fixes $a$ and the sign of $f'$ is the sign of the quadratic $q$.
solution: $f'$ changes $+\to-$ at $x=-\frac23$ (local maximum) and $-\to+$ at $x=1$ (local minimum). Option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Second-derivative test: at a root $x_0$ of $f'=e^xq$, $f''(x_0)=e^{x_0}q'(x_0)$.
solution: $f''(x)=e^x\left(q(x)+q'(x)\right)$; at a root of $q$ this is $e^{x}q'(x)$ with $q'(x)=6x-1$.
At $x=-\frac23$: $f''\left(-\frac23\right)=e^{-2/3}(-4-1)=-5e^{-2/3}<0$, so a local maximum. Same answer (B).

useful_results: If $f=e^{x}p(x)$, then $f'=e^{x}(p+p')$: the exponential never changes a sign, so only the polynomial $p+p'$ matters.
At a root $x_0$ of $f'=e^{x}q$, $f''(x_0)=e^{x_0}q'(x_0)$; the second term vanishes because $q(x_0)=0$.
For $f'=k(x-r_1)(x-r_2)$ with $k>0$ and $r_1<r_2$: maximum at $r_1$, minimum at $r_2$.
Check the roots: $q(1)=3-1-2=0$ and $q\left(-\frac23\right)=\frac43+\frac23-2=0$.

questions.question: The area (in sq. units) of the largest rectangle $ABCD$ whose vertices $A$ and $B$ lie on the $x$-axis and vertices $C$ and $D$ lie on the parabola $y=x^2-1$ below the $x$-axis, is:
questions.key_idea: By symmetry take $A(\alpha,0)$, $B(-\alpha,0)$, $D(\alpha,\alpha^2-1)$; the area is $2\alpha(1-\alpha^2)$.
solution: $AB=2\alpha$ and $AD=1-\alpha^2$ (the point $D$ is below the axis).

alternate_solutions.idea: AM-GM on $S^2=4u(1-u)^2$ with $u=\alpha^2$, using weights so that the sum of the three factors is constant.
solution: Write $u(1-u)^2=\frac12(2u)(1-u)(1-u)$; the three factors have constant sum $2u+(1-u)+(1-u)=2$.

useful_results: Largest rectangle with base on the axis inside $y=1-x^2$: half-width $\frac1{\sqrt3}$, height $\frac23$ of the depth, area $\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}\approx0.770$. The height ratio $\frac23$ holds for any parabolic segment.
For a product like $u(1-u)^2$, AM-GM with weights (here $2u,\,1-u,\,1-u$) gives the maximum without calculus.
Use symmetry to reduce a two-variable rectangle problem to one variable.
Check: $\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ gives $S=2(0.5774)(1-\frac13)=0.7698=\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}$.

questions.question: If the tangent to the curve $y=x^3$ at the point $P(t,t^3)$ meets the curve again at $Q$, then the ordinate of the point which divides $PQ$ internally in the ratio $1:2$ is:
questions.key_idea: Slope of the tangent at $P$ equals the slope of chord $PQ$; this gives $Q=(-2t,-8t^3)$.
solution: Let $Q(\alpha,\alpha^3)$. Slope of the tangent at $P$: $3t^2$; slope of chord $PQ$: $\frac{t^3-\alpha^3}{t-\alpha}$.
The point $R$ dividing $PQ$ internally in the ratio $1:2$ has ordinate $y_R=\frac{1\cdot y_Q+2\cdot y_P}{1+2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the tangent line, factor $x^3-(\text{line})$ as $(x-t)^2(x+2t)$, and note $R$ has abscissa $0$, so it is the tangent's $y$-intercept.
solution: Intersection with the curve: $x^3-3t^2x+2t^3=0$, which factors as $(x-t)^2(x+2t)=0$.
The double root $x=t$ is the point of contact; the other root $x=-2t$ gives $Q$.
$R$ lies on the tangent, so $y_R=3t^2(0)-2t^3=-2t^3$. Same answer.

useful_results: A tangent meets a cubic again at one more point: for $y=x^3+px^2+qx+r$ the tangent at $x=t$ meets it again at $x=-p-2t$ (sum of roots, with $t$ counted twice). For $y=x^3$ it is $-2t$.
Section formula: the ordinate dividing $P_1P_2$ internally in $m:n$ is $\frac{my_2+ny_1}{m+n}$.
On $y=x^3$ the point dividing the tangent chord $PQ$ in $1:2$ always has $x=0$, so it is the $y$-intercept of the tangent, $(0,-2t^3)$.

concepts: Mean value theorem (existence of a point)
questions.question: Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$, which are continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$. Then for every $f$ in $S$, there exists a $c\in(0,1)$, depending on $f$, such that:
questions.answer: None of (A)-(D) holds for every $f$ (the printed key says (C))
questions.key_idea: A claim 'for every $f$' is tested on the simplest members of $S$: a constant and $f(x)=x^2$.
solution: We need an option true for every $f\in S$; a single counterexample kills an option.
(B) $0<0$, (C) $0<0$ are false. (D) $|2k|<0$ is false for every $k$. So (B), (C), (D) fail for constants.
For a constant function (A) reads $0=0$, which is true, so (A) needs a different test.
Take $f(x)=x^2\in S$: (A) says $\frac{1-c^2}{1-c}=2c$, i.e. $1+c=2c$, so $c=1$, which is not in $(0,1)$. (A) fails.
Also for $f(x)=x^2$, (C) reads $1-c^2<2c(1-c)$, i.e. $1+c<2c$, i.e. $c>1$: false again.
Hence no option holds for every $f\in S$; the printed key (C) is incorrect (answer: none of the options).
questions.correction_note: The PDF says all four options fail for a constant function and then gives answer (C). That is inconsistent (the key contradicts its own working), and option (A) actually holds for a constant function (0 = 0). Correct reasoning: constants kill (B), (C), (D); f(x)=x^2 kills (A) and (C). So no option is true for every f in S, and the printed key (C) looks wrong.
useful_results: To refute 'for every $f$ in the class' try the extreme members first: a constant, a linear function, $x^2$, and a function not differentiable at an endpoint such as $\sqrt{1-x}$.
A strict inequality involving $|f'(c)|$ always fails for a constant function ($0<0$).

LMVT gives only $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=f'(c)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$; moving one end to $c$ (as in (A)) is not guaranteed, because Rolle's theorem needs the auxiliary function to be differentiable at both ends.
Check: for $f=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, $\frac{f(1)-f(c)}{1-c}=1+c$ equals $f'(c)=2c$ only at $c=1\notin(0,1)$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be a function of $x$ satisfying $y\sqrt{1-x^2}=k-x\sqrt{1-y^2}$ where $k$ is a constant and $y\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac14$. Then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $x=\frac12$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The relation is $\sin(\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y)=k$, so $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y$ is constant.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $x=\sin A$, $y=\sin B$: the relation becomes $\sin(A+B)=k$, so $A+B$ is constant and $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
solution: Let $x=\sin A$, $y=\sin B$ with $A,B\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, so $\cos A=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $\cos B=\sqrt{1-y^2}$.
The relation becomes $\sin B\cos A+\sin A\cos B=k$, i.e. $\sin(A+B)=k$.
Near the given point $\cos(A+B)\ne0$, so $A+B$ is locally constant: $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y=\text{const}$.

useful_results: $y\sqrt{1-x^2}+x\sqrt{1-y^2}=k$ means $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y=$ constant, so $y'=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
$xy-\sqrt{(1-x^2)(1-y^2)}=k$ means $\cos^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}y=$ constant, so $y'=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ (the same result).
Another pattern: $x\sqrt{1+y}+y\sqrt{1+x}=0$ gives $y=-\frac{x}{1+x}$ and $y'=-\frac{1}{(1+x)^2}$.
Expressions $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ signal the substitution $x=\sin A$ or $\cos A$. Numerical check: a finite-difference slope at $x=\frac12$ gives $-1.1180=-\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$.

questions.question: A $2$ m ladder leans against a vertical wall. If the top of the ladder begins to slide down the wall at the rate $25$ cm/sec., then the rate (in cm/sec.) at which the bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall on the horizontal ground when the top of the ladder is $1$ m above the ground is:
questions.key_idea: Differentiate $x^2+y^2=L^2$ in time: $x\dot x+y\dot y=0$, with $\dot y=-25$ when $y=1$.
solution: Let the foot be $x$ m from the wall and the top $y$ m high: $x^2+y^2=4$.
Given $\frac{dy}{dt}=-25$ (cm/s, the top is moving down) at the instant $y=1$ m.

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise by the angle $\theta$ with the ground: $x=2\cos\theta$, $y=2\sin\theta$.
solution: Let the ladder make angle $\theta$ with the ground: $x=2\cos\theta$, $y=2\sin\theta$.
$\frac{dy}{dt}=2\cos\theta\,\dot\theta=-25$ gives $\sqrt3\,\dot\theta=-25$, so $\dot\theta=-\frac{25}{\sqrt3}$ (per second, with the units of $y$).

useful_results: Sliding ladder: $\dot x=-\frac{y}{x}\dot y=-\dot y\tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle with the ground ($\tan\theta=\frac yx$).
The two speeds are equal in size exactly when $x=y$ (ladder at $45^\circ$).
As $y\to0$ the foot speed $\dot x\to\infty$ in this model, so the model breaks down near the ground.
Here $\tan\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\dot x=25\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}$; the ratio $\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\approx0.577$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=e^x-x$ and $g(x)=x^2-x$, $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then the set of all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, where the function $h(x)=(f\circ g)(x)$ is increasing, is:
questions.key_idea: $h'=(2x-1)\left(e^{x^2-x}-1\right)$ and $e^u-1$ has the sign of $u$, so $h'\ge0$ needs $(2x-1)$ and $(x^2-x)$ of the same sign.
solution: $h$ is increasing where $h'\ge0$: $A$ and $B$ are both $\ge0$ or both $\le0$.
Both non-positive: $x\le\frac12$ and $0\le x\le1$ gives $0\le x\le\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Composition rule: $h=f\circ g$ increases where $f$ and $g$ move the same way, using $f$ decreasing on $(-\infty,0]$ and increasing on $[0,\infty)$.
solution: $f'(u)=e^u-1$: $f$ is decreasing for $u\le0$ and increasing for $u\ge0$.
$g(x)=x^2-x$ has vertex at $x=\frac12$: decreasing on $\left(-\infty,\frac12\right]$, increasing on $\left[\frac12,\infty\right)$; and $g\ge0$ iff $x\le0$ or $x\ge1$.
$h$ is increasing where ($g\ge0$ and $g$ increasing) or ($g\le0$ and $g$ decreasing).
First case: $g\ge0$ and $x\ge\frac12$: $x\ge1$. Second case: $g\le0$ ($0\le x\le1$) and $x\le\frac12$: $0\le x\le\frac12$.

useful_results: $e^{u}-1$ has the same sign as $u$ for all real $u$; so $\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{g}-g\right)=g'(e^{g}-1)$ has the sign of $g\,g'$.
For a composition $h=f\circ g$: $h'=f'(g)\,g'$; $h$ increases where the two factors have the same sign.
$e^x-x$ is decreasing on $(-\infty,0]$ and increasing on $[0,\infty)$, with minimum value $1$ at $0$.
Include the points where $h'=0$ ($0,\frac12,1$): the function is still increasing across them, so the intervals are closed.

questions.question: Let $y(x)=(1+x)(1+x^2)(1+x^4)(1+x^8)(1+x^{16})$. Then $y'-y''$ at $x=-1$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Multiply by $(1-x)$: the product telescopes to $(1-x)y=1-x^{32}$, which is easy to differentiate twice.

alternate_solutions.idea: The product equals $1+x+x^2+\dots+x^{31}$ (binary expansion), so differentiate the polynomial term by term and use an alternating sum of squares.
solution: Every integer $0\le k\le31$ has a unique binary form, so $y=\sum_{k=0}^{31}x^k$.
Pair terms: $(2m+1)^2-(2m)^2=4m+1$ for $m=1,\dots,15$, plus the first term $1$: total $=1+\sum_{m=1}^{15}(4m+1)=1+4\cdot120+15=496$.

useful_results: $(1+x)(1+x^2)(1+x^4)\cdots(1+x^{2^{n-1}})=\frac{1-x^{2^n}}{1-x}=1+x+\dots+x^{2^n-1}$ (every exponent $0,\dots,2^n-1$ appears once, by binary expansion).

When a product is awkward to differentiate, find an equation it satisfies, e.g. $(1-x)y=1-x^{32}$, and differentiate that implicitly; the $m$-th differentiation gives $(1-x)y^{(m)}-my^{(m-1)}=-\frac{32!}{(32-m)!}x^{32-m}$.

concepts: Monotonicity and differentiability of a function
questions.question: Let $f(x)=x\cos^{-1}(-\sin|x|)$, $x\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$, then which of the following is true?
options: $f'$ is increasing in $\left(-\frac\pi2,0\right)$ and decreasing in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$
$f'$ is decreasing in $\left(-\frac\pi2,0\right)$ and increasing in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$
questions.key_idea: $\cos^{-1}(-t)=\frac\pi2+\sin^{-1}t$ and $\sin^{-1}(\sin|x|)=|x|$ on $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$, so $f=x\left(\frac\pi2+|x|\right)$.
solution: $f(x)=\frac{\pi x}{2}+x^2$ for $0\le x\le\frac\pi2$ and $f(x)=\frac{\pi x}{2}-x^2$ for $-\frac\pi2\le x<0$.
At $0$ both pieces give slope $\frac\pi2$, so $f$ is differentiable at $0$ and $f'(0)=\frac\pi2$; (B) and (C) are false.
So $f'$ is increasing in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ and decreasing in $\left(-\frac\pi2,0\right)$. Option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate $f$ directly by the product rule: $f'(x)=\cos^{-1}(-\sin|x|)+|x|$, then read off its shape.
solution: $\frac\pi2+2|x|$ is a V-shape with minimum at $0$: decreasing on $\left(-\frac\pi2,0\right)$, increasing on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$. Same answer (D).

useful_results: $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)=\theta$ only for $\theta\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$; here $\theta=|x|$ is in range, so no reduction is needed.
$x|x|$ is differentiable at $0$ with derivative $0$ and has derivative $2|x|$ everywhere, so $f=\frac{\pi}{2}x+x|x|$ is $C^1$ but has no second derivative at $0$.
Check: $f(x)=\frac{\pi x}{2}+x|x|$ is odd, so $f'$ is even; $f'(x)=\frac\pi2+2|x|$ has value $\frac\pi2$ at $0$.

questions.question: Let $f(\theta)=3\left(\sin^4\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin^4(3\pi+\theta)\right)-2\left(1-\sin^22\theta\right)$ and $S=\left\{\theta\in[0,\pi]:f'(\theta)=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right\}$. If $4\beta=\sum_{\theta\in S}\theta$, then $f(\beta)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Reduce $f$ to $\frac54-\frac14\cos4\theta$, so $f'=\sin4\theta$; the set $S$ solves $\sin4\theta=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF wrote the general solution as 4theta = n*pi + (-1)^n * pi/3, which solves sin4theta = +sqrt3/2, not -sqrt3/2. It then listed S = {pi/12, pi/6, 7pi/12, 2pi/3} (sum 3pi/2, beta = 3pi/8). The correct general solution is 4theta = n*pi + (-1)^n * (-pi/3); S = {pi/3, 5pi/12, 5pi/6, 11pi/12}, sum 5pi/2, beta = 5pi/8. Both routes give f(beta)=5/4 (cos(3pi/2)=cos(5pi/2)=0), so the key (D) is right by coincidence of the cosine value.

alternate_solutions.idea: Avoid listing roots: roots of $\sin4\theta=c$ pair up as $4\theta_1+4\theta_2=\pi+\dots$ (using $\sin x=\sin(\pi-x)$), so the sum of $\theta$ follows from the pairs.
solution: $f(\theta)=\frac54-\frac{\cos4\theta}4$, so we need only $\cos4\beta$ and $\sum\theta$ with $\sin4\theta=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

With $\varphi=4\theta\in[0,4\pi]$, $\sin\varphi=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ has two roots in each period $[2\pi m,2\pi(m+1)]$, symmetric about the minimum at $\varphi=\frac{3\pi}2+2\pi m$; so each pair sums to $3\pi+4\pi m$.

useful_results: $\sin^4\theta+\cos^4\theta=1-\frac12\sin^22\theta=\frac34+\frac14\cos4\theta$. Check $\theta=\frac\pi4$: $\frac14+\frac14=\frac12$ and $\frac34-\frac14=\frac12$.
Even powers remove signs and shifts by multiples of $\pi$: $\sin^4(3\pi+\theta)=\sin^4\theta$, $\sin^4\left(\frac{3\pi}2-\theta\right)=\cos^4\theta$.
General solution of $\sin\varphi=s$ is $\varphi=n\pi+(-1)^n\sin^{-1}s$; keep the sign of $s$ (here $\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=-\frac\pi3$).
Roots of $\sin\varphi=s$ in each period pair as $\varphi$ and $\pi-\varphi$, so sums of roots can be written without finding every root.

questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function satisfying $f'(3)+f'(2)=0$. Then $\lim_{x\to0}\left(\frac{1+f(3+x)-f(3)}{1+f(2-x)-f(2)}\right)^{1/x}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A $1^\infty$ limit is $e^{L}$ with $L=\lim\frac{u-1}{x}$; here $L$ is built from $f'(3)$ and $f'(2)$ by the definition of derivative.
solution: The base tends to $\frac{1+0}{1+0}=1$ and the exponent $\frac1x\to\infty$: form $1^\infty$.
By the definition of the derivative the bracket tends to $f'(3)+f'(2)$ (the second quotient is $\frac{f(2-x)-f(2)}{-x}\to f'(2)$).
$f$ is differentiable, hence continuous, so $1+f(2-x)-f(2)\to1$ and the second limit is $1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF applies L'Hopital's rule to the 0/0 form, giving f'(3+x)+f'(2-x) and then substitutes x=0. That needs f' to be continuous at 3 and 2, which is not given (f is only differentiable). Replaced by the definition of the derivative on each difference quotient. The answer 1 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Take logarithms and use the first-order expansion $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(h)$ with $\ln(1+u)\sim u$.

useful_results: $1^\infty$ form: $\lim u^{v}=e^{\lim(u-1)v}$ (when $u\to1$, $v\to\infty$ and the limit in the exponent exists).
For a merely differentiable $f$ use $f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(h)$ instead of L'Hopital on $f'$; L'Hopital needs $\lim f'(a+x)=f'(a)$.
More generally $\left(\frac{1+\alpha x+o(x)}{1+\beta x+o(x)}\right)^{1/x}\to e^{\alpha-\beta}$; here $\alpha=f'(3)$, $\beta=-f'(2)$, so the limit is $e^{f'(3)+f'(2)}$.
Check with $f(x)=(x-2.5)^2$ ($f'(3)=1$, $f'(2)=-1$): the expression at $x=10^{-5}$ equals $1.0000$.

questions.question: The absolute minimum value, of the function $f(x)=|x^2-x+1|+[x^2-x+1]$, where $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer function, in the interval $[-1,2]$, is:
questions.key_idea: $g=x^2-x+1\ge\frac34>0$, so $|g|=g$ and both $g$ and $[g]$ are smallest at the vertex $x=\frac12$.
solution: Thus $f(x)=g(x)+[g(x)]$, and both $g$ and $[g]$ are non-decreasing functions of $g$.
So both are smallest where $g$ is smallest, i.e. at $x=\frac12$ (the vertex).

alternate_solutions.idea: Lower-bound directly: $[g]\ge0$ gives $f\ge g\ge\frac34$, and equality is attained at $x=\frac12$.
solution: Equality needs $g=\frac34$ (so $x=\frac12\in[-1,2]$) and $[g]=0$, both true at $x=\frac12$.

useful_results: For $t\ge0$: $[t]\ge0$ and $[t]=0$ on $[0,1)$; a sum $t+[t]$ of two non-decreasing functions of $t$ is minimised where $t$ is.
$x^2-x+1$ is always $\ge\frac34$ (positive definite quadratic), so the modulus can be dropped.
Max of $f$ on $[-1,2]$: $g(-1)=g(2)=3$, so $f=3+3=6$ at the ends.

concepts: Higher-order derivatives of a logarithmic function
questions.question: Let $f:S\to S$ where $S=(0,\infty)$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(x+1)=xf(x)$. If $g:S\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $g(x)=\log_ef(x)$, then the value of $|g''(5)-g''(1)|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Take $\log$ of $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ and differentiate twice: $g''(x+1)-g''(x)=-\frac{1}{x^2}$, then telescope.

alternate_solutions.idea: Iterate the functional equation first: $f(x+4)=x(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)f(x)$, then differentiate $\ln f(x+4)$ twice once.
solution: Put $x=1$: $g''(5)-g''(1)=-\left(1+\frac14+\frac19+\frac1{16}\right)=-\frac{205}{144}$, so the modulus is $\frac{205}{144}$. Same answer.

useful_results: For $f(x+1)=xf(x)$ (the Gamma-type relation): $g=\ln f$ satisfies $g''(x+n)-g''(x)=-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(x+k)^2}$.
Telescoping: $g''(n+1)-g''(1)=-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1{k^2}$.
For $f=\Gamma$, $g''(1)=\frac{\pi^2}{6}$ and $g''(5)=\frac{\pi^2}6-\frac{205}{144}\approx0.2213$, matching $\psi_1(5)\approx\frac15+\frac1{50}+\frac1{750}$.

questions.question: If the function $f$ given by $f(x)=x^3-3(a-2)x^2+3ax+7$, for some $a\in\mathbb{R}$ is increasing in $(0,1]$ and decreasing in $[1,5)$, then a root of the equation $\frac{f(x)-14}{(x-1)^2}=0\ (x\ne1)$ is:
questions.key_idea: $f$ turns from increasing to decreasing at $x=1$, so $f'(1)=0$, which fixes $a$.
solution: $f$ increases on $(0,1]$ and decreases on $[1,5)$, so $f'$ changes sign at $x=1$: $f'(1)=0$.
Then $f(x)=x^3-9x^2+15x+7$ and $f'(x)=3(x-1)(x-5)$: positive on $(0,1)$ and negative on $(1,5)$, consistent with the data.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $f(1)=14$ and $f'(1)=0$, $f(x)-14$ has a double root at $1$; the third root comes from the sum of roots.
solution: $f(x)-14$ vanishes at $x=1$ and so does its derivative: $x=1$ is a double root.
Write $f(x)-14=(x-1)^2(x-r)$; the sum of the three roots $=1+1+r=3(a-2)=9$ (coefficient of $x^2$ is $-9$).
$r=7$, so $\frac{f(x)-14}{(x-1)^2}=x-7$ and the root is $7$. Same answer.

useful_results: If a differentiable $f$ switches from increasing to decreasing at $c$, then $f'(c)=0$ (a local maximum); this fixes unknown parameters.
If $f(c)=m$ and $f'(c)=0$, then $(x-c)^2$ divides $f(x)-m$; the remaining factor follows from the sum or product of roots.
For a monic cubic $x^3+px^2+qx+r$ the sum of roots is $-p$; here $-p=3(a-2)=9$.

questions.question: The set of all real values of $\lambda$ for which the function $f(x)=(1-\cos^2x)(\lambda+\sin x)$, $x\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, has exactly one maxima and exactly one minima, is:
questions.key_idea: $f'=\sin x\cos x\,(2\lambda+3\sin x)$: two sign-changing zeros, $x=0$ and $\sin x=-\frac{2\lambda}3$, are needed in the open interval.
solution: A second critical point needs $-\frac{2\lambda}3\in(-1,1)$, i.e. $-2\lambda\in(-3,3)$, so $\lambda\in\left(-\frac32,\frac32\right)$.
It must differ from $x=0$: $\sin x=-\frac{2\lambda}3\ne0$, so $\lambda\ne0$.

For $\lambda\in\left(-\frac32,\frac32\right)\setminus\{0\}$ there are two distinct critical points where $f'$ changes sign: one maximum and one minimum. (For $\lambda=0$, $f=\sin^3x$ is monotonic; for $|\lambda|\ge\frac32$ only $x=0$ is critical.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $t=\sin x$ (strictly increasing on the interval): extrema of $f$ correspond to extrema of the cubic $p(t)=\lambda t^2+t^3$ on $(-1,1)$.
solution: $t=\sin x$ maps $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ increasingly onto $(-1,1)$, so $f$ and $p(t)=\lambda t^2+t^3$ have the same number and type of extrema.
A cubic has one maximum and one minimum exactly when $p'$ has two distinct (simple) roots; both must lie in $(-1,1)$.

useful_results: A strictly monotonic substitution ($t=\sin x$ on $(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)$) preserves extrema, so $\sin x$-polynomials reduce to ordinary polynomials in $t$ on $(-1,1)$.
A cubic $p$ has a local max and a local min iff $p'$ has two distinct real roots; a double root of $p'$ (e.g. $t^3$) gives an inflection, not an extremum.
Roots of $p'$ outside the open interval give no interior extremum; end points are excluded here.

Check: $\lambda=1$: $p=t^2+t^3$ has a maximum at $t=-\frac23$ and a minimum at $t=0$; numerical sign scan found exactly 2 turning points for $\lambda=\pm1,\pm0.1$ and 1 for $|\lambda|\ge1.5$, 0 for $\lambda=0$.
